title: Linked List Fundamentals
summary: Node structure, singly/doubly/circular variants, and the core insert/delete operations every list problem builds on — plus why you'd ever pick pointers over a contiguous array.

slides.markdown:
A **linked list** is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node. No contiguous memory block, no fixed size, no index arithmetic — just pointers.

That one design choice flips the array's trade-offs upside down: insertion and deletion at a known position become O(1) instead of O(n), but random access becomes O(n) instead of O(1). Nearly every list interview question is really asking whether you understand that swap.

This group builds from raw node manipulation up to the design questions (LRU-style structures, random-pointer copying) that lean on it.

slides.subTitle: How next and prev chain into a list
slides.markdown:
A node is a small object: a `value` field plus one or more pointer fields. A **singly linked list** node has just `next`; a **doubly linked list** node has `next` and `prev`; a **circular list** wires the last node's `next` back to the first instead of to null.

The list itself is usually just a `head` pointer (and often a `tail` pointer for O(1) append). Everything else is reachable by walking `next` from there.

<<< Image: three small diagrams side by side — a singly linked list of four boxes with arrows only pointing right and a final arrow to a null symbol; a doubly linked list with arrows pointing both right (next) and left (prev) between each pair of boxes; a circular list of four boxes where the last box's arrow loops back to the first box instead of to null >>>

slides.subTitle: Memory cost, traversal direction, and when each wins
slides.markdown:
| Variant | Extra memory | Traversal | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Singly | 1 pointer/node | forward only | stacks, simple queues, most interview problems |
| Doubly | 2 pointers/node | both directions | LRU caches, deques, undo/redo, text editors |
| Circular | same as base type | wraps around | round-robin schedulers, circular buffers, Josephus-style problems |

Doubly linked costs 50–100% more memory per node (an extra pointer, often 8 bytes on a 64-bit machine) in exchange for O(1) removal of a node you're already holding, without needing its predecessor. That's exactly the property an LRU cache's linked list relies on.

Circular isn't really a separate storage layout — it's a wiring choice on top of singly or doubly linked, useful whenever "after the last comes the first" is a real property of the problem.

Deleting or inserting at the **head** of a list is a special case: there's no predecessor to update, so code that handles "delete node at position i" ends up with a separate branch for i = 0.

The fix: allocate one extra **sentinel node** before the real head, and point your `head` reference at the sentinel instead of the first real node. Every real node — including the first — now has a predecessor. The special case disappears; insert-before and delete-at-position become the same code path regardless of position.

You unwrap it at the end by returning `sentinel.next` instead of `head`. This single trick removes more edge-case bugs from list problems than any other technique in this group.

Given a reference to a node, inserting **after** it never touches any other node:

```python
def insert_after(node, value):
    new_node = Node(value)
    new_node.next = node.next
    node.next = new_node
```

Inserting **before** a given node (without a predecessor pointer) is the harder case in a singly linked list — you can't reach backward. The usual trick: copy the given node's value forward into a new node, then overwrite the given node's own value and `next` with the new data. Effectively you insert "after" and then swap values, so it *looks* like you inserted before.

Inserting at the head is just `new_node.next = head; head = new_node` — O(1), no dummy needed for this specific operation.

slides.sectionTitle: Deleting a node given only that node
slides.markdown:
A classic interview constraint: you're handed a node reference, not the head, and asked to delete it — with no way to walk backward to find its predecessor.

The trick: you can't unlink the node itself, but you can make it **disappear** by copying the next node's data into it, then unlinking the next node instead.

```python
def delete_node(node):
    # node is guaranteed not to be the tail
    node.val = node.next.val
    node.next = node.next.next
```

This fails if `node` is the last node — there's nothing to copy forward from, which is exactly why interviewers state that guarantee explicitly. Flag it back to them if the constraint is missing.

slides.subTitle: The classic dangling-pointer bug
slides.markdown:
The single most common list bug: overwriting `node.next` before you've saved a copy of the old value somewhere you still need it.

```python
# BUG: next is now gone before we use it
node.next = new_node
old_next = node.next  # this is new_node, not the original next!
```

Any operation that needs "where this pointer used to point" — reversal, insertion, deletion, splicing two lists together — must capture that value into a local variable **before** the assignment that overwrites it. The fix is one line: `old_next = node.next` *before* `node.next = new_node`. It looks trivial until you're three pointers deep in a reversal and lose track of ordering.

slides.subTitle: Checking the wrong node to stop
slides.markdown:
A circular list has no null to stop at, so a traversal loop needs an explicit termination condition — and the natural-looking one is often wrong.

```python
# BUG: never terminates if head has more than one node,
# because curr never becomes None in a circular list
curr = head
while curr is not None:
    process(curr)
    curr = curr.next
```

The fix is to stop on **returning to a known node**, not on hitting null: `curr = head; while True: process(curr); curr = curr.next; if curr is head: break`. Watch the empty-list and single-node cases too — a size-0 or size-1 circular list needs its own check before the loop starts, or you process a node zero or infinite times.

Every linked-list decision comes back to one exchange: **O(1) insertion/deletion at a known node, paid for with O(n) access to an arbitrary position.**

An array lets you jump to index k in O(1) because the memory is contiguous — the address is `base + k * element_size`. A linked list has no such formula; reaching the kth node means walking k pointers from the head, because nodes can live anywhere in memory.

This is also why linked lists are cache-unfriendly: each `next` hop can be a pointer into a different, unrelated page of memory, while an array scan reads sequential bytes the CPU already prefetched. Two structures with the same Big-O for traversal (both O(n)) can differ 5–10x in wall-clock time for exactly this reason — see the `complexity` group's discussion of what Big-O deliberately ignores.

slides.subTitle: What an interviewer is really testing when they ask you to choose
slides.markdown:
| Operation | Dynamic array | Singly linked list |
|---|---|---|
| Random access by index | O(1) | O(n) |
| Insert/delete at known position | O(n) (shift elements) | O(1) once there |
| Insert/delete at end | amortized O(1) | O(1) with tail pointer |
| Cache behavior | excellent (contiguous) | poor (scattered) |
| Memory overhead | none per element | one+ pointer per element |

When an interviewer asks "array or linked list for this?", they're testing whether you reach for the structure that matches the **access pattern**, not the one you're more comfortable coding. Frequent random reads by index, or a need for cache-friendly bulk scans → array. Frequent insert/delete in the middle given a reference, or an unknown/streaming size → linked list.

In practice, production code reaches for a linked list far less often than interview problems suggest — most "linked list" real-world needs (LRU order, deques) are served by a doubly linked list wrapped inside a library type, not hand-rolled.
